subject: Geography
title: Year 9 Geography Exam 1
topic: Megadisasters · Supervolcanoes, tsunamis, atmospheric circulation, weather and tropical storms
intro: Section A is a quick quiz (Q1-14). Section B (Q15-20) asks you to describe and explain processes: write them as steps in the right order and use the key words (low pressure, condenses, Coriolis effect, caldera). Section C (Q21-22) needs your case studies from your book: use real places, dates and numbers, sort effects into immediate and long-term, and finish Q22 with a clear judgement. Spend about 20 minutes on Section C.

questions.q:
Section A: Quiz
An event is a megadisaster if it causes at least one of four things. Which of these is one of them?
options: GDP of a country lowered by 1%
questions.ms: B1: Over 2000 deaths. (The others: 200,000 people homeless; GDP lowered by more than 5%; depending on aid from abroad for over 1 year.)

questions.q: How is an oceanic plate different from a continental plate?
options: It is thicker and less dense
It is thinner and more dense
It is thicker and more dense
It is thinner and less dense
questions.ms: B1: Oceanic plates are thinner and denser (heavier); continental plates are thicker and less dense.

questions.q: The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) goes from 1 to 8. Each time you go up one step, the power of the eruption...
questions.ms: B1: Increases by 10 times (x10).

questions.q: A supervolcano is a volcano that has had an eruption with a VEI of what number?
questions.ms: Answer: 8. B1. (It also erupts more than 1,000 km³ of material.)

questions.q: A supervolcano is wide and flat, with a large depression in the middle where the land collapsed into the empty magma chamber. What is this depression called?
questions.ms: Answer: a caldera. B1. Accept small spelling slips such as 'caldara' if marking by hand.

questions.q: Why do volcanoes in a hotspot island chain (like Hawaii) eventually go extinct?
options: The magma plume runs out of magma
The ocean cools the magma chamber
The plate moves them away from the hotspot
questions.ms: B1: The plate keeps moving, so each volcano is carried off the hotspot and has no more magma supply.

questions.q: Why is a tsunami hardly noticeable out in the open ocean?
options: The ocean is deep enough to carry the energy, so the wave is low
It only forms near the coast
questions.ms: B1: The ocean is deep enough to carry the energy, so the wave height is small. It grows as the sea gets shallower.

questions.q: In the Hadley cell, air sinks at about 30°N and 30°S. What does this create?
options: Low pressure, clouds and tropical rainforests
High pressure, clear skies and deserts
questions.ms: B1: Sinking air gives high pressure, clear skies and deserts.

questions.q: On a barometer, high pressure is a reading above how many millibars (mb)?
questions.ms: Answer: 1016 mb. B1.

questions.q: Which instrument uses spinning cups to measure wind speed?
questions.ms: Answer: anemometer. B1. (A weather vane shows wind direction; a barometer measures air pressure.) Accept small spelling slips such as 'anenometer' if marking by hand.

questions.q: Tropical storms need warm oceans. What is the minimum sea temperature needed, in °C?
questions.ms: Answer: 26.5 °C. B1. (They also need water at least 50 m deep and the Coriolis effect.)

questions.q: Where do tropical storms form?
options: Between 5° and 30° north and south of the equator
questions.ms: B1: Between 5° and 30° N/S, near the equator but not on it (there is no Coriolis effect on the equator).

questions.q: In a tropical storm, where is the strongest band of wind and rain?
options: Far out at sea, ahead of the storm
questions.ms: B1: The eye wall, the first band around the calm eye.

questions.q: Warm air meets cold air. The cold air is denser, so it pushes the warm air upwards and rain clouds form along the boundary. Which type of rainfall is this?
questions.ms: B1: Frontal rainfall (the boundary is called a front).

questions.q:
Section B: Describe and explain
Describe how a hotspot creates a chain of volcanic islands, such as Hawaii.
questions.ms: 1 mark per point, max 3, in a sensible order. A plume of magma under the crust melts the plate above it [1]. Magma erupts onto the surface slowly and cools, building a shield volcano / island [1]. The plate moves over the hotspot but the plume stays still [1], so the plume does the same again and makes a new volcano [1], creating a chain of islands; the older ones have moved off the hotspot and are extinct [1]. 3 marks needs the idea that the plate moves and the hotspot does not.

questions.q: Explain how a supervolcano forms. Use the word caldera in your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark per linked step, max 4. A magma chamber is fed with magma over a hotspot [1]. The chamber fills and is under too much pressure [1]. It erupts through many fissures (cracks) in the surface, causing a massive super eruption, VEI 8 / over 1,000 km³ of material [1]. The land collapses into the now empty magma chamber [1], creating a depression called a caldera [1]. 4 marks needs the caldera step explained (land collapses into the empty chamber), not just the word.

questions.q: Explain how a tsunami forms and why it becomes so dangerous when it reaches the coast.
questions.ms: Levels. L2 (3-4): a linked sequence: an underwater disturbance, e.g. an underwater earthquake, displaces (moves) the water and gives energy to the wave; out at sea the wave is low because the deep ocean carries the energy; as it approaches land the sea becomes shallower so the wave height increases; friction with the ocean floor slows the base and makes the wave even taller until it hits the coastline. 4 marks needs both the trigger AND a reason the wave grows near the coast (shallower water or friction). L1 (1-2): one or two simple points, e.g. 'caused by an earthquake', 'the wave gets bigger'.

questions.q: Use the Hadley cell to explain why there are tropical rainforests at the equator but deserts at about 30°N and 30°S.
questions.ms: 2 marks for rainforests + 2 marks for deserts. Rainforests: air at the equator receives more intense radiation from the Sun, gets hotter and rises, creating low pressure [1]; it reaches the top of the atmosphere, cools and condenses into clouds, so it rains a lot [1]. Deserts: the air splits and travels to 30°N/S, where it cools slightly and sinks [1], creating high pressure with clear skies, so there is little rain [1]. Stating 'low pressure = rain, high pressure = dry' with no rising/sinking air: max 1 per half.

questions.q: Explain how a tropical storm forms. You should refer to the three conditions needed.
questions.ms: Levels, 6 marks. L3 (5-6): a full, linked explanation in order. Conditions: ocean at least 26.5 °C, water at least 50 m deep, Coriolis effect (so between 5-30° N/S, not on the equator). Process: intense evaporation from deep, warm ocean water makes rising air and an area of low pressure; the Coriolis effect makes the rising air spin (anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere, clockwise in the southern); as the air rises and spins it cools and condenses into towering cumulonimbus clouds; some air at the top sinks in the middle to form the calm, clear eye, surrounded by the eye wall with the strongest wind and rain. L2 (3-4): most steps, but some links missing, or the conditions are only partly given. L1 (1-2): simple points, e.g. 'warm water evaporates and makes clouds'. Key words that lift an answer: evaporation, low pressure, Coriolis effect, condenses, cumulonimbus, eye, eye wall.

questions.q: Explain how relief rainfall forms and why the land behind the mountain stays dry.
questions.ms: 1 mark per point, max 3. Warm, moist air from the sea is forced to rise over mountains [1]. As it rises it cools and condenses, forming clouds, so it rains on that side of the mountain [1]. The air then descends on the other side and warms, so it has lost its moisture and there is little rain, creating a rain shadow [1]. 3 marks needs the term rain shadow or a clear description of it.

questions.q:
Section C: Case studies
Yellowstone, in the USA, is a supervolcano. Describe the likely immediate and long-term effects if Yellowstone were to have a super eruption.
questions.ms: Levels, 6 marks (use your Week 2B work). L3 (5-6): several effects, clearly sorted into immediate and long-term, with detail and range (people, economy, environment; USA and the world), and some explanation of why each happens. L2 (3-4): a mix of immediate and long-term effects with some detail, but unbalanced or not explained. L1 (1-2): one or two general effects, e.g. 'lots of people die'. Indicative content. Immediate: pyroclastic flows and lava destroy everything close to the volcano and kill people nearby; thick ash falls across much of the USA, collapsing roofs and blocking roads; flights grounded across North America; ash contaminates water supplies and causes breathing problems; crops and livestock in the Midwest farming area are buried; millions must evacuate. Long-term: ash and gas in the atmosphere block sunlight, causing a 'volcanic winter' and colder global temperatures for years; crop failures cause global food shortages and rising food prices; the US economy is badly damaged, which hits the world economy; huge numbers of people are made homeless and migrate; the USA could depend on aid, making it a megadisaster on every criterion.

questions.q:
For a tsunami OR a tropical storm you have studied:
"The long-term effects were more serious than the immediate effects."
How far do you agree? Use your case study to explain your answer.

Name your case study and the year at the start of your answer.
questions.ms: Levels, 9 marks (use Week 5A for the tsunami or Week 9A for the tropical storm). L3 (7-9): names a real case study with accurate, specific facts (place, date, numbers); explains both immediate and long-term effects; compares them (how many people affected, for how long, cost, whether the country recovered); reaches a clear, supported judgement on 'how far'. L2 (4-6): describes immediate and long-term effects with some case-study facts; some comparison or a judgement that is stated but not well supported. L1 (1-3): general effects of any disaster with few or no case-study facts; no real judgement. Max 4 if there is no named case study. Indicative content (credit the case study used in class). Japan, 11 March 2011: magnitude 9.0 underwater earthquake; waves up to about 40 m; around 18,000 dead or missing; hundreds of thousands evacuated or homeless; Fukushima nuclear power plant meltdown (immediate leak, long-term exclusion zone and clean-up lasting decades); about $235 billion cost, the most expensive disaster recorded; Japan, a rich country, rebuilt quickly. Indian Ocean, 26 December 2004: magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra; about 230,000 deaths in 14 countries, Aceh (Indonesia) worst hit; about 1.7 million homeless; long-term loss of fishing boats and tourism jobs, salt water ruined farmland, disease risk from dirty water, countries depended on foreign aid for years; it led to an Indian Ocean warning system. Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines, 8 November 2013: winds over 300 km/h, storm surge about 5 m, over 6,000 deaths, around 4 million people displaced, Tacloban destroyed; long-term homelessness, lost crops and fishing, years of rebuilding. Hurricane Katrina, USA, 2005: about 1,800 deaths, New Orleans levees failed and 80% of the city flooded, about $125 billion damage, many people never returned. Credit any well-argued judgement, e.g. 'immediate effects were worse in Japan because a rich country rebuilt quickly, but long-term effects were worse in Indonesia because poor fishing communities lost their livelihoods'.
